newsitem.title: FRANCE: Investigators see progress in Paris bomb probe.
newsitem.headline: Investigators see progress in Paris bomb probe.

text.p: Investigators reported progress on Thursday in their probe into the bombing of a Paris rush-hour commuter train as police flanked by troops patrolled French cities and borders in hopes of preventing any fresh attacks.

Investigators believe they have determined where the perpetrator had boarded the train as well as his route, enabling them better to pinpoint where they should search for additional witnesses, sources close to the probe said.

Police appealed to travellers who used the suburban line around the time of Tuesday's blast, which killed two people, to get in touch, and set up a freephone number after questioning dozens of witnesses.

Interior Minister Jean-Louis Debre pointed to "extremely worrying similarities" between the attack and a spate of bomb blasts last year claimed by Moslem fundamentalist rebels fighting Algeria's French-backed military government.
"There are similarities not only in the make-up of the device but also in the methods used," he told Radio Luxembourg.

Investigators focused on Algerian militants, battling the French-backed military government in a war that has claimed an estimated 50,000 lives since 1992 when Algiers scrapped elections that Islamic fundamentalists were poised to win.
The daily Le Monde said the bombers used an electronic timer from a cooker as a detonator, slightly more sophisticated than the alarm clocks with metal hands used in last year's bombs.
In other ways, the bomb was identical to the 1995 devices, stuffed into a hollowed-out gas canister with nails.

In a high-profile show of strength designed to reassure and deter, soldiers and police guarded railway stations in Paris and major cities, and tightened surveillance at borders, airports and tourist sites like the Eiffel Tower.

A total of 1,870 troops and 1,700 paramilitary gendarmes were ordered out to back up police, including 800 in Paris. French customs agents were also asked to help out by tightening security at borders, ports, airports and railway stations.

Spot checks were made on cars on the Champs-Elysees avenue and guards at stores searched Christmas shoppers' bags. Police handed stickers to travellers on the Metro underground railway urging them to watch out for suspect packages.
Trains resumed on the RER suburban line where the bomb exploded during Tuesday's evening rush-hour at Port Royal station.

Twenty-two people were still in hospital on Thursday after the blast, which killed two people and injured 91. The dead were a newly-married Canadian woman, Helene Viel, and a Frenchman from New Caledonia, Lucien Devambez.

Viel had just arrived in Paris on Sunday with her husband, Frank Stonebanks, to search for a flat. Her husband was to be transferred on January 1 from Montreal to the French capital by his employer, U.S. pharmaceutical firm Rhone-Poulenc Rorer.

Prime Minister Alain Juppe met Debre for a briefing on the the so-called Vigipirate plan, reimposed after the 1995 blasts claimed by the radical Algerian Armed Islamic Group (GIA) that killed eight and wounded more than 160.
Debre said France had been at "constant risk" since last year and that investigators had kept up probes and arrests. "There are today almost 200 Islamists in prison," he said.
He dismissed press suggestions that France had had warnings of imminent attacks.
